column4: The rebuke asks why the hearers اثَّاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ, became heavy toward the earth; this exactly realizes the source section's dictionary gloss for the earth-root branch rather than merely repeating its noun.

The man who could have been raised instead أَخْلَدَ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ, clinging downward to earth; that moral lowering gives a Quranic counterpart to the source section's dictionary sense of settling heavily toward the ground.
God says فَإِذَا سَوَّيْتُهُ before breathing spirit into the human; the same root denotes the completed bodily forming that stands behind the section's proportioned self.
The repeated creation formula فَإِذَا سَوَّيْتُهُ again joins exact human fashioning with the divine breath, confirming this formative use of s-w-y.
After 82:7's creating, proportioning, and balancing, this ayah says God assembled the person in whatever form He willed; it contributes the particular configuration produced by formative sewwā.
God created people and strengthened their frame, yet can replace them at will; bodily construction and removal are explicitly held together under one power.
Mountains that appear fixed pass like clouds, while the ayah names this the workmanship of God who perfected everything; stable height and exact workmanship meet in one divine act.
Among the judged towns, some remain standing and some are حَصِيدٌ, mown down; the contrast directly renders settlements either upright or reduced like a reaped field.
God says many wrongdoing towns were قَصَمْنَا, shattered, and another people raised after them; communal breaking and replacement closely express the section's eradication sense.
فَقُطِعَ دَابِرُ الْقَوْمِ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا states that the last remnant of the wrongdoing people was cut off, a direct Quranic formulation of the source section's istiʾṣāl gloss.
The blast rightfully seizes the wrongdoers and makes them غُثَاءً, washed-up debris; a whole people is reduced to discarded matter as Thamūd is to crushed straw.
God destroys what Pharaoh and his people manufactured and what they raised on trellises; constructed and cultivated works are brought down together.
A town's affluent people rebel and the town is destroyed utterly; culpability within inhabited prosperity leads to total demolition just as sin leads to Thamūd's leveling.
ʿĀd and Thamūd are named, and their dwellings remain evident to the audience after their deeds led them away; surviving habitation makes the absent peoples' overthrow visible.
Travelers are told to see the predecessors' end: God destroyed what was over them; the wording makes ruin descend upon a formerly established people and their world.
God casts down the overturned towns, a compact scene of habitation and people made to fall from high to low.
God rolls up the sky and promises to repeat creation as He began it; cosmic unmaking and exact re-creation are expressly works of the same agent.
God saves Hūd and those with him while cutting off the last remnant of the deniers; this comparative judgment joins total eradication to an explicit moral distinction among people.
The earth appears humbled and lifeless, then stirs and grows when water descends; the same ground-state that resembles leveling becomes evidence that the giver of life can raise the dead.
The doomed townspeople are told to return to their luxury and dwellings; this identifies the inhabited prosperity that 21:15 turns into a reaped, extinguished community.
The passage identifies ʿĀd and the barren wind sent against them, supplying the agent whose reducing action 51:42 describes.
ʿĀd are destroyed by a furious, violent wind; this ayah identifies the force that leaves the bodies fallen like hollow trunks in 69:7.
The question "How were My punishment and warnings?" makes divine warning and consequence the explicit bridge between the single hamstringer in 54:29 and the community's reduction in 54:31.
The audience is asked how many generations were destroyed before them and told those peoples do not return; this supplies the irreversible communal absence following the single cry.
The monumental peoples just named, including Thamūd, are identified as those who transgressed in the lands; the ayah supplies the shared cause of their fall.
Those same peoples multiplied corruption in the lands, extending the causal account from impressive building to destructive conduct.
The Lord pours upon the named peoples a scourge of punishment, completing the sequence that begins with Thamūd's rock-cut landscape in 89:9.
Thamūd's secure setting includes gardens and springs; this is part of the inhabited abundance within which 26:149's mountain houses seem permanent.
Crops and laden palms further specify the cultivated plain surrounding Thamūd's carved houses, sharpening what is lost when the people are seized.
The residents of al-Ḥijr deny the messengers; this identifies the stance of the very rock-house dwellers whose security and overthrow 15:82-83 stage.
Pharaoh orders a lofty structure built so that he can challenge Moses' God; elevated construction becomes a concrete expression of the pride answered in 28:40.
God seizes Pharaoh and his forces and casts them into the sea, completing the movement from the self-exalting tower of 28:38 to collective overthrow.
The decree concerning Lot's people is that their last remnant will be cut off by morning; it is another precise Quranic formulation of root-and-branch eradication.
Thamūd are explicitly included among successive peoples who rejected, placing their fate in a wider series of demolished communities.
Each of those peoples received clarifying examples and each was destroyed completely; the ayah supplies the totalizing end of the Thamūd-inclusive list in 25:38.
